documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

  Doe, Jamie

  A1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. Cell phones, PDA’s, or cameras may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Do not discuss the contents of this exam with anyone until after March 27th.
- Good luck!

transcription.notes: Six top-level problems A1–A4 (Part A) and B1–B2 (Part B), emitted as numbers 1–6 with the printed labels as titles. Problem points are the sums of the printed part points (no per-problem total is printed); paper total is not printed. A2 and B2 have printed lettered divisions (a./b.) with roman-numbered sub-questions, transcribed as sections; A2 b. has no sub-questions and is a section without parts. Printed point markers such as “(13 pts)” and “(5)” are carried in the points fields. Printed errors kept verbatim in the official solutions: (A2-5) exponent 5/3 (should be 3/5 from A2-4); A2 b solution uses δr for the Δr of the statement; (A4-8) ε0 appears in the numerator of the final expression; (B1-17) printed “n(2mgsin)/k” with θ missing; (B2-6) uses r in (z^2 + r^2) where R is meant; (B2-10) m = eω0R/2 (R² expected from B2-9); (B2-19) printed “b_0” for B_0; B2 b.v writes N δm and then Δm; in B1 d the parenthesis opened before “because the equilibrium shifts up” is never closed. In the problem statement of B2 a.i the printed text is “(k is the Coulomb’s Law constant).”; A2 a.ii prints “Assume, instead that” without a second comma — kept. The constants table on page 1 prints ε_o and μ_o with subscript o; kept. No spelling fixes were needed.

problems.title: A1
problems.statement: A group of 12 resistors is arranged along the edges of a cube as shown in the diagram below. The vertices of the cube are labeled $a$-$h$.

figures.alt: A cube drawn in perspective with a resistor on each of its 12 edges; the vertices are labeled a, b, c, d (upper), e, f, g, h (lower): a–b, a–c, a–e, c–d, b–d, c–g, b–f, d–h, e–f, e–g, g–h, f–h.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement:
The resistance between each pair of vertices is as follows:

$R_{ab} = R_{ac} = R_{ae} = 3.0\ \Omega$

$R_{cg} = R_{ef} = R_{bd} = 8.0\ \Omega$

$R_{cd} = R_{bf} = R_{eg} = 12.0\ \Omega$

$R_{dh} = R_{fh} = R_{gh} = 1.0\ \Omega$

What is the equivalent resistance between points $a$ and $h$?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: The three $12.0\ \Omega$ resistors are replaced by identical capacitors. $C_{cd} = C_{bf} = C_{eg} = 15.0\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. A $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery is attached across points $a$ and $h$ and the circuit is allowed to operate for a long period of time. What is the charge ($Q_{cd}$, $Q_{bf}$, $Q_{eg}$) on each capacitor after this long period of time?

answer.note: The same charge on each of the three capacitors.

solution.statement:
a. There is a high degree of symmetry present. Points $b$, $c$, and $e$ are at the same potential; similarly, points $d$, $f$, and $g$ are at the same potential. The circuit then reduces to a series connection of three parallel resistor clusters.

The three parallel clusters have effective resistances of $1\ \Omega$, $8/5\ \Omega$, and $1/3\ \Omega$. The effective resistance of the circuit is then $44/15\ \Omega$.

b. After a long time no current will flow through the branches of the circuits containing capacitors. The circuit then reduces to a parallel connection of three series resistor clusters.

The effective resistance of the circuit is $4\ \Omega$, the current through the circuit is then

$$(12\ \mathrm{V})/(4\ \Omega) = 3\ \mathrm{A}. \tag{A1-1}$$

The three branches are identical; each then carries $1\ \mathrm{A}$.

The potential drop across each capacitor is the same as the potential drop across the $8\ \Omega$ resistors, so

$$V_C = (1\ \mathrm{A})(8\ \Omega) = 8\ \mathrm{V}. \tag{A1-2}$$

Finally, the charge on each capacitor is

$$Q = (15\ \mu\mathrm{F})(8\ \mathrm{V}) = 120\ \mu\mathrm{C}. \tag{A1-3}$$

problems.title: A2
problems.statement: A simple gun can be made from a uniform cylinder of length $L_0$ and inside radius $r_c$. One end of the cylinder is sealed with a moveable plunger and the other end is plugged with a cylindrical cork bullet. The bullet is held in place by friction with the walls of the cylinder. The pressure outside the cylinder is atmospheric pressure, $P_0$. The bullet will just start to slide out of the cylinder if the pressure inside the cylinder exceeds $P_{cr}$.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement: There are two ways to launch the bullet: either by heating the gas inside the cylinder and keeping the plunger fixed, or by suddenly pushing the plunger into the cylinder. In either case, assume that an ideal monatomic gas is inside the cylinder, and that originally the gas is at temperature $T_0$, the pressure inside the cylinder is $P_0$, and the length of the cylinder is $L_0$.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Assume that we launch the bullet by heating the gas without moving the plunger. Find the minimum temperature of the gas necessary to launch the bullet. Express your answer in terms of any or all of the variables: $r_c, T_0, L_0, P_0$, and $P_{cr}$.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: Assume, instead that we launch the bullet by pushing in the plunger, and that we do so quickly enough so that no heat is transferred into or out of the gas. Find the length of the gas column inside the cylinder when the bullet just starts to move. Express your answer in terms of any or all of the variables: $r_c, T_0, L_0, P_0$, and $P_{cr}$.

answer.note: As printed in the official solution (A2-5). From (A2-4), P_0 L_0^γ = P_cr L^γ with γ = 5/3, the exponent should be 3/5; the printed 5/3 is kept verbatim.

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
It is necessary to squeeze the bullet to get it into the cylinder in the first place. The bullet normally has a radius $r_b$ that is slightly larger than the inside radius of the cylinder; $r_b - r_c = \Delta r$, is small compared to $r_c$. The bullet has a length $h \ll L_0$. The walls of the cylinder apply a pressure to the cork bullet. When a pressure $P$ is applied to the bullet along a given direction, the bullet’s dimensions in that direction change by

$$\frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{-P}{E}$$

for a constant $E$ known as Young’s modulus. You may assume that compression along one direction does not cause expansion in any other direction. (This is true if the so-called Poisson ratio is close to zero, which is the case for cork.)

If the coefficient of static friction between the cork and the cylinder is $\mu$, find an expression for $P_{cr}$. Express your answer in terms of any or all of the variables: $P_0, \mu, h, E, \Delta r$, and $r_c$.

answer.note: Part b, official solution (A2-9); the solution writes δr for the printed Δr of the statement.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Two parts, solved individually.

i. Isochoric compression:

$$\frac{P_f}{P_i} = \frac{T_f}{T_i}, \tag{A2-1}$$

so

$$T = \frac{P_{cr}}{P_0}T_0. \tag{A2-2}$$

ii. Adiabatic compression:

$$PV^{\gamma} = \mathrm{const}, \tag{A2-3}$$

where $\gamma = C_P/C_V = (C_V + 1)/C_V = 5/3$ for a monatomic gas. Consequently

$$P_0 L_0^{\gamma} = P_{cr} L^{\gamma}, \tag{A2-4}$$

and then

$$L = L_0\left(\frac{P_0}{P_{cr}}\right)^{5/3}. \tag{A2-5}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The normal pressure on the bullet comes from

$$P = \frac{\delta r}{r_c}E. \tag{A2-6}$$

Therefore, the normal force on the bullet is

$$F_N = \frac{\delta r}{r_c}E \times (2\pi r_c h), \tag{A2-7}$$

and finally the force of friction is $\mu F_N$. The force due to the pressure difference between the inside of the barrel and the outside must equal the normal force, so

$$(\pi r_c^2)(P_{cr} - P_0) = 2\pi h\mu\ \delta r\ E, \tag{A2-8}$$

and then

$$P_{cr} = P_0 + \frac{2\mu E h}{r_c^2}\delta r. \tag{A2-9}$$

problems.title: A3
problems.statement: A volume $V_f$ of fluid with uniform charge density $\rho$ is sprayed into a room, forming spherical drops. As they float around the room, the drops may break apart into smaller drops or coalesce into larger ones. Suppose that all of the drops have radius $R$. Ignore inter-drop forces and assume that $V_f \gg R^3$.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Calculate the electrostatic potential energy of a single drop. (Hint: suppose the sphere has radius $r$. How much work is required to increase the radius by $dr$?).

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the total electrostatic energy of the drops?
parts.statementAfter: Your answer to (b) should indicate that the total energy increases with $R$. In the absence of surface tension, then, the fluid would break apart into infinitesimally small drops. Suppose, however, that the fluid has a surface tension $\gamma$. (This value is the potential energy per unit surface area, and is positive.)

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What is the total energy of the drops due to surface tension?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: What is the equilibrium radius of the drops?

solution.statement:
a. If the sphere has radius $r$, it has charge

$$q = \frac{4}{3}\pi\rho r^3 \tag{A3-1}$$

and thus its surface is at electrostatic potential

$$V = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} = \frac{\rho r^2}{3\epsilon_0} \tag{A3-2}$$

To increase the radius by $dr$, an additional charge $dq = 4\pi r^2 dr$ must be brought in from infinity, requiring work

$$dU = V\,dq\ = \frac{4\pi r^4\rho^2}{3\epsilon_0}dr \tag{A3-3}$$

Thus to grow the sphere from $r = 0$ to $r = R$ requires

$$U = \int_0^R \frac{4\pi r^4\rho^2}{3\epsilon_0}dr = \frac{4\pi R^5\rho^2}{15\epsilon_0} \tag{A3-4}$$

b. Each drop has volume $V_d = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$, so the number of drops is

$$n = \frac{V_f}{V_d} = \frac{V_f}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} \tag{A3-5}$$

Since we are ignoring inter-drop forces, the total energy of the drops is simply the sum of the energies of each individual drop:

$$U_{e,tot} = nU = \frac{V_f}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}\frac{4\pi R^5\rho^2}{15\epsilon_0} = \frac{R^2\rho^2}{5\epsilon_0}V_f \tag{A3-6}$$

c. Each drop has surface area $4\pi R^2$ and thus surface tension energy $4\pi R^2\gamma$. As before, the total energy due to surface tension is just the sum of the energies of the individual drops:

$$U_{s,tot} = 4\pi R^2\gamma n = 4\pi R^2\gamma\frac{V_f}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{3\gamma}{R}V_f \tag{A3-7}$$

d. The total potential energy from both sources is

$$U_{tot} = \left(\frac{R^2\rho^2}{5\epsilon_0} + \frac{3\gamma}{R}\right)V_f \tag{A3-8}$$

Equilibrium is reached when the total energy is a minimum; since $U \to \infty$ at both $R \to 0$ and $R \to \infty$, it must have an interior minimum.

$$\frac{d}{dR}U_{tot} = \left(\frac{2R\rho^2}{5\epsilon_0} - \frac{3\gamma}{R^2}\right)V_f \tag{A3-9}$$

Setting this equal to zero,

$$\frac{2R\rho^2}{5\epsilon_0} = \frac{3\gamma}{R^2} \tag{A3-10}$$

$$R^3 = \frac{15\gamma\epsilon_0}{2\rho^2} \tag{A3-11}$$

$$R = \left(\frac{15\gamma\epsilon_0}{2\rho^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \tag{A3-12}$$

problems.title: A4
problems.statement: A nonlinear circuit element can be made out of a parallel plate capacitor and small balls, each of mass $m$, that can move between the plates. The balls collide inelastically with the plates, dissipate all kinetic energy as thermal energy, and immediately release the charge they are carrying to the plate. Almost instantaneously, the balls then pick up a small charge of magnitude $q$ from the plate; the balls are then repelled directly toward the other plate under electrostatic forces only. Another collision happens, kinetic energy is dissipated, the balls give up the charge, collect a new charge, and the cycle repeats. There are $n_0$ balls per unit surface area of the plate. The capacitor has a capacitance $C$. The separation $d$ between the plates is much larger than the radius $r$ of the balls. A battery is connected to the plates in order to maintain a constant potential difference $V$. Neglect edge effects and assume that magnetic forces and gravitational forces may be ignored.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Determine the time it takes for one ball to travel between the plates in terms of any or all of the following variables: $m$, $q$, $d$, and $V$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Calculate the kinetic energy dissipated as thermal energy when one ball collides inelastically with a plate surface in terms of any or all of the following variables: $m$, $q$, $d$, and $V$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the current between the plates in terms of the permittivity of free space, $\varepsilon_0$, and any or all of the following variables: $m$, $q$, $n_0$, $C$, and $V$.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the effective resistance of the device in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, and any or all of the following variables: $m$, $q$, $n_0$, $C$, and $V$.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Calculate the rate at which the kinetic energy of the balls is converted into thermal energy in terms of $\varepsilon_0$, and any or all of the following variables: $m$, $q$, $n_0$, $C$, and $V$.

answer.note: As printed in the official solution (A4-8): ε0 appears in the numerator of the final expression, while the preceding step gives C/ε0; the printed form is kept verbatim.

solution.statement:
a. The electric field between the plates is given by $E = V/d$. The force on the charged ball is then $F = Eq = Vq/d$. The acceleration of the ball is $a = Vq/md$.

Kinematics gives us $d = at^2/2$ for the time of flight. So

$$t = \sqrt{2d/a} = \sqrt{2md^2/qV}. \tag{A4-1}$$

b. The kinetic energy collected by a ball will be $K = qV$ as it moves between the plates. That’s what will be dissipated.

c. The current is given by $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$. The total number of balls is $N = n_0 A$, where $A$ is the surface area of a plate. The charge $\Delta Q$ is then $\Delta Q = n_0 q A$, so the current is

$$I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \frac{n_0 q A}{\sqrt{2md^2/qV}}. \tag{A4-2}$$

We can’t stop here, since this is *not* in terms of the allowed variables. The problem is $A$ and $d$, but since $C = \epsilon_0 A/d$, we have

$$I = \frac{n_0 q A}{\sqrt{2md^2/qV}}, \tag{A4-3}$$

$$= \frac{A}{d}n_0 q\sqrt{\frac{qV}{2m}}, \tag{A4-4}$$

$$= \frac{C}{\epsilon_0}n_0 q\sqrt{\frac{qV}{2m}}. \tag{A4-5}$$

d. $R = V/I$, so

$$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{\epsilon_0 V}{Cn_0q}\sqrt{\frac{2m}{qV}}. \tag{A4-6}$$

We can simplify, slightly, with

$$R = \frac{\epsilon_0}{Cn_0q}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}}. \tag{A4-7}$$

e. $P = VI$, so

$$P = V\frac{C}{\epsilon_0}n_0 q\sqrt{\frac{qV}{2m}} = \sqrt{\frac{{\epsilon_0}^2{n_0}^2C^2q^3V^3}{2m}}. \tag{A4-8}$$

problems.title: B1
problems.statement: A certain mechanical oscillator can be modeled as an ideal massless spring connected to a moveable plate on an incline. The spring has spring constant $k$, the plate has mass $m$, and the incline makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. When the system is operating correctly, the plate oscillates between points $A$ and $B$ in the figure, located a distance $L$ apart. When the plate reaches point $A$ it has zero kinetic energy, but then trips a small lever that instantaneously loads a block of mass $M$ onto the plate. The block and plate then move down the incline to point $B$, where the force from the spring stops the plate. At this point, the block falls through a hole in the incline, allowing the plate to move back up under the force of the spring. Upon returning to point $A$ it collects another block, and the cycle repeats. Both the plate and the block have a coefficient of friction $\mu$ with the incline for both kinetic and static friction. It is reasonable that the motion in either direction is simple harmonic in nature.

figures.alt: An incline rising to the right. At the bottom left a spring (labeled “spring”) pushes a moving plate (labeled “moving plate”, arrow) at point B; just above B there is a gap in the incline labeled “blocks fall here”. At the top right, at point A, a square block sits on a horizontal ledge labeled “blocks load here”.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Let $\mu_c$ be the critical value of the coefficient of friction where the block will just start to slide under the force of gravity on an incline (without the spring acting on it). Then let $\mu = \frac{\mu_c}{2}$. Find $\mu$ in terms of $g$, the acceleration of free fall, and any or all of the following variables: $\theta$ and $M$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: In order for this system to work correctly, it is necessary to have the correct ratio between the mass of the block and the mass of the plate. These masses are chosen so that the downward moving block and plate just stop at point $B$ while the upward moving plate just stops at point $A$. Find the ratio $R = \frac{M}{m}$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: The system delivers blocks to point $B$ with period $T_0$, until the blocks run out. After that, the plate alone oscillates with a period $T'$. Find the ratio $\frac{T_0}{T'}$.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: The plate only oscillates a few times after delivering the last block. At what distance up the incline, measured from point $B$, does the plate come to a permanent stop?

answer.note: Stopping points at n(2mg sin θ)/k and L − n(2mg sin θ)/k; the plate stops at the first of these for which n(2mg sin θ)/k > L/2 or (n + 1/2)(2mg sin θ)/k > L/2.

solution.statement:
a. To not slip, from a free-body diagram, we must have

$$\mu mg\cos\theta \geq mg\sin\theta \tag{B1-1}$$

so

$$\mu \geq \tan\theta. \tag{B1-2}$$

Therefore $\mu_c = \tan\theta$ and hence

$$\mu = \frac{\tan\theta}{2}. \tag{B1-3}$$

b. In one cycle the energy input into the system is

$$MgL\sin\theta, \tag{B1-4}$$

the energy of the block dropping.

The energy loss on the way up is

$$L\mu mg\cos\theta \tag{B1-5}$$

and the energy loss on the way down is

$$L\mu(m + M)g\cos\theta \tag{B1-6}$$

Thus

$$MgL\sin\theta = L\mu mg\cos\theta + L\mu(m + M)g\cos\theta \tag{B1-7}$$

and since $2\mu\cos\theta = \sin\theta$,

$$M = \frac{m}{2} + \frac{m + M}{2}, \tag{B1-8}$$

$$= 2m, \tag{B1-9}$$

$$R = M/m = 2. \tag{B1-10}$$

c. The period of a mass $m$ oscillating on a spring of spring constant $k$ is

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}. \tag{B1-11}$$

In this case, the friction force is constant on both the up and down trips, and so each trip is simple harmonic (with different equilibrium points). Hence

$$T_0 = \pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} + \pi\sqrt{\frac{3m}{k}}, \tag{B1-12}$$

$$T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \tag{B1-13}$$

$$T_0/T' = \frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}. \tag{B1-14}$$

d. As mentioned in part (c), both the up and down trips are simple harmonic, this time with a mass of $m$ both ways. The equilibrium points for the two trips are different, however. On the up trip, the equilibrium point is clearly at a distance $L/2$ from $B$, since the plate stops at both $B$ and $A$ and hence those are the endpoints of the oscillation and the equilibrium is halfway between. For the trip down, the equilibrium point will shift by a distance $y$ such that

$$ky = 2\mu mg\cos\theta = mg\sin\theta \tag{B1-15}$$

because $2\mu mg\cos\theta$ is the difference between the friction forces on the trip up and the trip down.

The place where the plate finally comes to a stop is the first place that is at the end of an oscillation (either up or down) and where the total force being exerted by gravity and the spring is less than the maximal force of friction. For that to happen, the plate needs to not have gone past the other equilibrium point during that oscillation.

So we start by determining where the endpoints of the oscillations are. For the first trip up these are $B$ and $A$. For the following trip down, the plate stops at a distance of $(2mg\sin\theta)/k$ from $B$ (because the equilibrium shifts up by $(mg\sin\theta)/k$. For the following trip up, the plate stops a distance $L - (2mg\sin\theta)/k$ from $B$, since the equilibrium point is again in the middle of the incline. And so forth.

Thus the stopping points are located at

$$n(2mg\sin\theta)/k \text{ and } L - n(2mg\sin\theta)/k \tag{B1-16}$$

for integer $n$. The plate will stop permanently once either

$$n(2mgsin)/k > L/2 \tag{B1-17}$$

or

$$L - n(2mg\sin\theta)/k < L/2 + (mg\sin\theta)/k, \tag{B1-18}$$

whichever happens first. (The first condition corresponds to going down and ending up above the midpoint at the end of the down trip, the second condition corresponds to going up and stopping below the upper equilibrium.) The second condition can be rewritten as

$$\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)(2mg\sin\theta)/k > L/2. \tag{B1-19}$$

problems.title: B2
problems.statement: A model of the magnetic properties of materials is based upon small magnetic moments generated by each atom in the material. One source of this magnetic moment is the magnetic field generated by the electron in its orbit around the nucleus. For simplicity, we will assume that each atom consists of a single electron of charge $–e$ and mass $m_e$, a single proton of charge $+e$ and mass $m_p \gg m_e$, and that the electron orbits in a circular orbit of radius $R$ about the proton.

sections.title: a. Magnetic Moments.
sections.statement: Assume that the electron orbits in the $x$-$y$ plane.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
Calculate the net electrostatic force on the electron from the proton. Express your answer in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e$, $m_e$, $m_p$, $R$, and the permittivity of free space, $\varepsilon_0$, where

$$\varepsilon_0 = \frac{1}{4\pi k}.$$

($k$ is the Coulomb’s Law constant).

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: Determine the angular velocity $\omega_0$ of the electron around the proton in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e$, $m_e$, $R$, and $\varepsilon_0$.

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the magnetic field $B_e$ due to the orbital motion of the electron at a distance $z \gg R$ from the $x$-$y$ plane along the axis of orbital rotation of the electron. Express your answer in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e$, $m_e$, $R$, $\omega_0$, $z$, and the permeability of free space $\mu_0$.

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement:
A small bar magnet has a magnetic field far from the magnet given by

$$B = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\frac{m}{z^3},$$

where $z$ is the distance from the magnet on the axis connecting the north and south poles, $m$ is the magnetic dipole moment, and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. Assuming that an electron orbiting a proton acts like a small bar magnet, find the dipole moment $m$ for an electron orbiting an atom in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e$, $m_e$, $R$, and $\omega_0$.

answer.note: As printed in the official solution (B2-10); substituting (B2-9) into the bar-magnet formula gives eω0R²/2, so the printed power of R is kept verbatim.

sections.title: b. Diamagnetism.
sections.statement: We model a diamagnetic substance to have all atoms oriented so that the electron orbits are in the $x$-$y$ plane, exactly half of which are clockwise and half counterclockwise when viewed from the positive $z$ axis looking toward the origin. Some substances are predominantly diamagnetic.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Calculate the total magnetic moment of a diamagnetic substance with $N$ atoms. Write your answer in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e, m_e, R, N$, and $\mu_0$.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: An external magnetic field $\vec{B}_0 = B_0\hat{z}$ is applied to the substance. Assume that the introduction of the external field doesn’t change the fact that the electron moves in a circular orbit of radius $R$. Determine $\Delta\omega$, the change in angular velocity of the electron, for both the clockwise and counterclockwise orbits. Throughout this entire problem you can assume that $\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0$. Write your answer in terms of $e, m_e$, and $B_0$ only.

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement: Assume that the external field is turned on at a constant rate in a time interval $\Delta t$. That is to say, when $t = 0$ the external field is zero and when $t = \Delta t$ the external field is $\vec{B}_0$. Determine the induced emf $\mathcal{E}$ experienced by the electron. Write your answer in terms of any or all of the following parameters: $e, m_e, R, N$, $B_0$, $\omega_0$, and $\mu_0$.

answer.note: The official solution (B2-19) prints the last factor as b_0 instead of B_0.

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement: Verify that the change in the kinetic energy of the electron satisfies $\Delta K = e\,\mathcal{E}$. This justifies our assumption in (ii) that $R$ does not change.

parts.label: v.
parts.statement: Determine the change in the total magnetic moment $\Delta m$ for the $N$ atoms when the external field is applied, writing your answer in terms of $e, m_e, R, N, \mu_0$ and $B_0$.

parts.label: vi.
parts.statement: Suppose that the uniform magnetic field used in the previous parts of this problem is replaced with a bar magnet. Would the diamagnetic substance be attracted or repelled by the bar magnet? How does your answer show this?

sections.title: a. Magnetic Moments
sections.statement:
i. From Coulomb’s Law,

$$F = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2} \tag{B2-1}$$

ii. For circular motion,

$$F = \frac{m_e v^2}{R} = m_e R\omega_0^2, \tag{B2-2}$$

The force is provided by the Coulomb force, so

$$m_e R\omega_0^2 = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2}, \tag{B2-3}$$

$$\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 m_e R^3}} \tag{B2-4}$$

iii. From the law of Biot and Savart,

$$\vec{B}_e = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi}\oint\frac{d\vec{s} \times \vec{r}}{r^3}, \tag{B2-5}$$

$$B_e = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi}2\pi R\frac{R}{(z^2 + r^2)^{3/2}}, \tag{B2-6}$$

$$\approx \frac{\mu_0 i R^2}{2z^3}. \tag{B2-7}$$

For the current, $i$, we can write

$$i = \frac{q}{t} = \frac{e\omega_0}{2\pi}. \tag{B2-8}$$

Then

$$B_e = \frac{\mu_0 e\omega_0 R^2}{4\pi z^3}. \tag{B2-9}$$

iv. By substitution,

$$m = \frac{e\omega_0 R}{2}. \tag{B2-10}$$

sections.title: b. Diamagnetism
sections.statement:
i. If half go one way and half go the other, $M = 0$.

ii. Additional force from magnetism,

$$F_B = qvB_0 = eR\omega B_0 \tag{B2-11}$$

modifies previous central force problem to give

$$m_e R\omega^2 = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R^2} \pm eR\omega_0 B_0, \tag{B2-12}$$

where the positive sign corresponds to anticlockwise motion, the negative to clockwise motion.

A little math,

$$m_e R(\omega^2 - \omega_0^2) = \pm eR\omega B_0, \tag{B2-13}$$

$$m_e(\omega - \omega_0)(\omega + \omega_0) = \pm e\omega B_0, \tag{B2-14}$$

$$m_e(\Delta\omega)(2\omega_0) = \pm e\omega_0 B_0, \tag{B2-15}$$

where in the last line we have used the approximation $\omega \approx \omega_0$. Then

$$\Delta\omega = \pm\frac{eB_0}{2m_e}. \tag{B2-16}$$

iii. The emf is given by

$$\mathcal{E} = n\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t}\Phi, \tag{B2-17}$$

but $\Delta n/\Delta t$ is a measure of the number of turns made by the electron in a time interval $\Delta t$, so

$$\frac{\Delta n}{\Delta t} = \frac{\omega_0 R}{2\pi R} = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}. \tag{B2-18}$$

Then

$$\mathcal{E} = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}B_0\pi R^2 = \frac{1}{2}\omega_0 b_0 R^2. \tag{B2-19}$$

iv. The change in kinetic energy is given by

$$\Delta K = \Delta\left(\frac{1}{2}m_e\omega^2R^2\right), \tag{B2-20}$$

$$= m_e R^2\omega\ \Delta\omega, \tag{B2-21}$$

$$\approx m_e R^2\omega_0\ \Delta\omega, \tag{B2-22}$$

$$= m_e\omega_0 R^2\left(\pm\frac{eB_0}{2m_e}\right), \tag{B2-23}$$

$$= e\mathcal{E}. \tag{B2-24}$$

v. $\Delta M = N\delta m$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, and $\Delta m$ the change in magnetic moment in each. The change is

$$\Delta m = \Delta\left(\frac{e\omega_0 R}{2}\right). \tag{B2-25}$$

$$= \frac{eR}{2}\Delta\omega, \tag{B2-26}$$

$$= \frac{e^2R^2B_0}{4m_e}, \tag{B2-27}$$

so

$$\Delta M = N\frac{e^2R^2B_0}{4m_e}. \tag{B2-28}$$

vi. Repelled, by Lenz’s law.
